title: Adjectives with Prepositions: People and Reactions
summary: Use adjective–preposition combinations to judge what someone did, describe treatment of other people, express feelings about events and results, and distinguish an apology from sympathy. The correct preposition depends on both the adjective and the meaning.
learningObjectives: Distinguish kind or careless of somebody from kind or rude to somebody.
Describe feelings about situations, feelings towards people and satisfaction with results.
Use at/by, with and of appropriately after surprised, impressed, fed up and tired.
Choose sorry about a situation, sorry for/about your own actions and sorry for someone needing sympathy.

explanation.heading: Judge a person’s action with of; describe treatment with to
explanation.body: Use it was kind, generous, polite, honest, foolish or careless of somebody to do something when you evaluate the person’s behaviour. Use be kind, polite, friendly, rude or cruel to somebody when you describe how another person was treated. The person after of performed the action; the person after to received the behaviour. Both patterns can appear in a single situation.
explanation.example: It was thoughtful of Hana to check on the visitors, and she was friendly to everyone.

explanation.heading: Feelings about an event versus feelings towards a person
explanation.body: Angry, annoyed, furious and upset commonly take about when you identify a situation or action causing the feeling. Use angry or annoyed with somebody for doing something to name the person responsible and the reason. For anticipation or concern, use excited, nervous, worried or happy about an event. Other prepositions can occur in English, but learn these clear intermediate-level patterns first.
explanation.example: Priya was annoyed with the organiser for changing the venue without warning.

explanation.heading: Use with for satisfaction and results
explanation.body: Pleased, satisfied, delighted, happy and disappointed commonly take with when judging something you received or experienced, such as a service, performance or result. With introduces the thing being evaluated. By contrast, happy about the upcoming trip expresses an emotional reaction to an event, not satisfaction with a finished outcome.
explanation.example: We were satisfied with the repaired bicycle after the test ride.

explanation.heading: Reactions to surprises and continuing irritation
explanation.body: Surprised, amazed and shocked can take at or by to introduce the cause of the reaction. Impressed can take with or by to name what made a strong positive impression. For an activity or situation that has become unpleasant through repetition, use fed up with or bored with; tired of shows you no longer want to keep experiencing something. These common chunks are best learnt together.
explanation.example: Owen was amazed by the final performance but bored with the long introduction.

explanation.heading: Separate an apology from sympathy
explanation.body: Sorry about usually introduces an unfortunate situation: sorry about the confusion. Sorry for or sorry about can refer to something you did: sorry for interrupting or sorry about interrupting. Feel sorry for somebody means you sympathise with a person who is having a hard time. Sorry for a person does not automatically mean you caused the person’s problem, so context matters.
explanation.example: I am sorry about the mix-up, and I feel sorry for the guests who missed the show.

comparisons.title: Who acted versus who was treated

left.label: generous of somebody
left.example: It was generous of Leo to donate the books.

right.label: generous to somebody
right.example: Leo was generous to the local library.

comparisons.title: Cause of irritation versus person responsible

left.label: annoyed about something
left.example: I am annoyed about the unexpected fee.
left.note: About names the issue that caused the feeling.

right.label: annoyed with somebody for something
right.example: I am annoyed with Ben for hiding the fee.
right.note: With names the person; for introduces what Ben did.

left.label: sorry about an incident
left.example: I am sorry about the booking error.
left.note: The speaker acknowledges an unfortunate situation.

right.label: sorry for a person
right.example: I feel sorry for the stranded travellers.
right.note: The speaker expresses sympathy for people in difficulty.

examples.sentence: It was honest of the cashier to report the extra payment.
examples.note: Honest of identifies a person whose behaviour is being judged.

examples.sentence: The guide was patient and polite to the youngest visitors.
examples.note: Polite to names the people who received considerate treatment.

examples.sentence: Karim is nervous about his first public presentation.
examples.note: Nervous about introduces a coming event that causes anxiety.

examples.sentence: The volunteers were delighted with the renovated community centre.
examples.note: Delighted with expresses satisfaction with a result.

examples.sentence: I was shocked at how quickly the tickets sold out.
examples.note: Shocked at identifies what produced the strong reaction; by is also possible.

examples.sentence: After three delays, the passengers were fed up with waiting.
examples.note: Fed up with expresses strong frustration at an ongoing situation.

examples.sentence: We felt sorry for the cyclist whose bike had been stolen.
examples.note: Sorry for introduces the person receiving sympathy.

commonMistakes.incorrect: It was very kind to Felix to bring us warm drinks.
commonMistakes.correct: It was very kind of Felix to bring us warm drinks.
commonMistakes.why: Felix performed the kind act, so judge his behaviour with kind of Felix.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Why were you so rude with the receptionist?
commonMistakes.correct: Why were you so rude to the receptionist?
commonMistakes.why: Rude to introduces the person who received the rude behaviour.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I am nervous for giving the presentation next week.
commonMistakes.correct: I am nervous about giving the presentation next week.
commonMistakes.why: Nervous about introduces an upcoming event that worries the speaker.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I feel sorry about the family who lost their home.
commonMistakes.correct: I feel sorry for the family who lost their home.
commonMistakes.why: Feel sorry for somebody expresses sympathy for people facing difficulty.

studyTips: When learning adjective pairs, write both the adjective and its role: kind of the helper, kind to the guest, angry about the problem, angry with the person.
Build a short contrast card with three uses of sorry: sorry about the delay, sorry for arriving late, and sorry for the people who waited.
Practise reporting a real or imagined event with one reaction about it, one judgement of a person’s behaviour, and one evaluation of the result.

exercises.prompt: It was generous ___ Mateo to offer his spare room to a stranded traveller.
exercises.feedback: Generous of Mateo judges the helpful action Mateo performed.

exercises.prompt: The receptionist was extremely polite ___ the visitors despite the delay.
exercises.feedback: Polite to identifies the people receiving polite treatment.

exercises.prompt: The trainees were very satisfied ___ the quality of the workshop.
exercises.feedback: Satisfied with evaluates a result or experience.

exercises.prompt: Amir is nervous ___ his driving test next Tuesday.
exercises.feedback: Nervous about introduces the upcoming test causing concern.

exercises.prompt: The children are excited ___ their first overnight school trip. (Supply one preposition.)
acceptedAnswers: about
exercises.feedback: Excited about introduces an event they are looking forward to.

exercises.prompt: After hearing what happened, I felt sorry ___ the injured dog. (Supply one preposition expressing sympathy.)
acceptedAnswers: for
exercises.feedback: Feel sorry for is used for a person or animal in difficulty.

exercises.prompt: We are fed up ___ receiving the same automated reply. (Supply one preposition.)
acceptedAnswers: with
exercises.feedback: Fed up with expresses frustration with a repeated experience.

exercises.prompt: She was very kind ___ the elderly passengers on the bus. (Supply one preposition for how people are treated.)
acceptedAnswers: to
exercises.feedback: Kind to introduces the people who received help or consideration.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: It was generous to us to offer our spare tickets to the guests.
acceptedAnswers: It was generous of us to offer our spare tickets to the guests.
exercises.feedback: We were the people who offered the tickets, so use generous of us to judge our action.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The supervisor was rude with the new employee during the meeting.
acceptedAnswers: The supervisor was rude to the new employee during the meeting.
exercises.feedback: Rude to identifies who was treated badly.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I am sorry of interrupting the discussion earlier.
acceptedAnswers: I am sorry for interrupting the discussion earlier.
I am sorry about interrupting the discussion earlier.
exercises.feedback: Sorry for or sorry about can introduce an action the speaker regrets; sorry of is not used.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We feel sorry about the people who lost their homes in the storm.
acceptedAnswers: We feel sorry for the people who lost their homes in the storm.
exercises.feedback: Feel sorry for someone expresses sympathy with people in a difficult situation.

speakingExercises.prompt: Eva helped carry the heavy bags. Judge her action in one sentence beginning 'It was kind', naming 'Eva', and ending 'to carry the heavy bags'.
acceptedAnswers: It was kind of Eva to carry the heavy bags.
speakingExercises.feedback: Of Eva identifies the person whose helpful act is being judged.

speakingExercises.prompt: The waiter treated the guests respectfully. Say one sentence beginning 'The waiter was polite' and ending 'the guests'.
acceptedAnswers: The waiter was polite to the guests.
speakingExercises.feedback: Polite to names the people receiving respectful treatment.

speakingExercises.prompt: Change the adjective phrase in 'Sam is worried for tomorrow’s examination.' to the standard pattern with about. Say the complete corrected sentence.
acceptedAnswers: Sam is worried about tomorrow’s examination.
speakingExercises.feedback: Worried about introduces the future event causing concern.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your team liked the finished design. Say one sentence beginning 'We were pleased' and ending 'the final design'.
acceptedAnswers: We were pleased with the final design.
speakingExercises.feedback: Pleased with evaluates a result the team received.

speakingExercises.prompt: Lea is upset because Hugo cancelled the appointment. Say 'Lea is annoyed', followed by Hugo as the person responsible, then 'for cancelling the appointment'.
acceptedAnswers: Lea is annoyed with Hugo for cancelling the appointment.
speakingExercises.feedback: Annoyed with introduces Hugo; for explains his action.

speakingExercises.prompt: You admired the singer’s performance. Say one sentence beginning 'I was impressed', using 'by', and ending 'the performance'.
acceptedAnswers: I was impressed by the performance.
speakingExercises.feedback: Impressed by gives the source of a favourable reaction; with would also be grammatical generally, but this prompt specifies by.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say these two facts as two sentences in order. First apologise for the confusion, beginning 'I am sorry'. Then sympathise with the disappointed guests, beginning 'I feel sorry'.
acceptedAnswers: I am sorry about the confusion. I feel sorry for the disappointed guests.
I’m sorry about the confusion. I feel sorry for the disappointed guests.
speakingExercises.feedback: Sorry about names a problem, while feel sorry for expresses sympathy for people.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say two short sentences, in this order, about one repeated task. First say 'I am fed up' + 'waiting'. Then say 'I am tired' + 'waiting'. Use the correct prepositions.
acceptedAnswers: I am fed up with waiting. I am tired of waiting.
I’m fed up with waiting. I’m tired of waiting.
I am fed up with waiting. I’m tired of waiting.
I’m fed up with waiting. I am tired of waiting.
speakingExercises.feedback: Fed up with and tired of are natural, different adjective–preposition patterns for frustration.

listeningExercises.audioText: It was generous of Mira to buy lunch for everyone. She was also especially kind to my father.
listeningExercises.feedback: Kind to my father identifies the person who received special consideration.

listeningExercises.audioText: I am annoyed with Theo for changing the plan without telling us. The short delay itself did not bother me.
choices: Theo changed the plan without warning
listeningExercises.feedback: Theo’s failure to tell the group about the change caused the annoyance, not the delay.

listeningExercises.audioText: The children were excited about opening the time capsule at the end of term.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word adjective–preposition expression immediately after "were".
acceptedAnswers: excited about
listeningExercises.feedback: Excited about introduces the event they were anticipating.

listeningExercises.audioText: We were satisfied with the new software, but shocked by how much the training cost.
listeningExercises.feedback: The software was satisfactory; the training price caused the shock.

listeningExercises.audioText: I feel sorry for the families whose homes were flooded. I am also sorry about the cancelled concert.
listeningExercises.prompt: Who is the speaker expressing sympathy for?
choices: The people who bought concert tickets
listeningExercises.feedback: Feel sorry for the families expresses sympathy towards those directly affected by the flood.

listeningExercises.audioText: Lina is bored with the training course, whereas Sam is nervous about the final assessment.
choices: Both are nervous about the course
Lina is pleased and Sam is bored
Lina lacks interest; Sam feels anxious
listeningExercises.feedback: Bored with shows Lina’s lack of interest, while nervous about describes Sam’s concern.

listeningExercises.audioText: It was unkind of the driver to shout at a passenger who asked for directions.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word judgement expression immediately after "was".
acceptedAnswers: unkind of
listeningExercises.feedback: Unkind of identifies whose behaviour the speaker is judging.

listeningExercises.audioText: I am tired of completing the same paperwork at the end of every shift.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word adjective–preposition expression immediately after "am".
acceptedAnswers: tired of
listeningExercises.feedback: Tired of expresses frustration with an unpleasant repeated activity.
